newsitem.title: USA: Ex-soldier to start defense for N.C. race murders.
newsitem.headline: Ex-soldier to start defense for N.C. race murders.

text.p: Defence lawyers for a former Army private on trial for murdering a black couple were due to begin their case Monday most likely by saying he lost control of himself because of heavy drinking.

Over the past two weeks the jury has heard James Burmeister, a former paratrooper in the U.S. Army's elite 82nd Airborne Division who has been linked to a white supremacist skinhead group, characterised as "pure, unmitigated evil" by prosecutors.
Burmeister, 21, is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of Jackie Burden and Michael James, shot as they walked through a neighbourhood Dec. 7, 1995.
Fayetteville is just outside of the Fort Bragg military installation, home to the 82nd Airborne.

Burmeister's lawyers Carl Ivarsson and Larry McGlothlin have not revealed their defence, but prosecutors said they were told an expert on "pathological intoxication" would testify about Burmeister's inability to control himself after excessive drinking the night of the killings.
Tom Foley, a former prosecutor who has tried various hate crimes, said if he was defending Burmeister, then he would rely on such a witness too.

"I would explore his mental state to try and determine if he set out to kill," he said. "I'd look for evidence that he either had a bad experience with blacks or that peer pressure was somehow to blame."
Burden, 27, and James, 36, were shot at point-blank range.
A DNA specialist testifying for the prosecution said blood found on Burmeister's clothing the day after the shootings matched Burden's and James' blood.
Prosecutors planned to seek the death penalty if a first-degree murder conviction is returned for Burmeister, of Thompson, Pa.

His friend Randy Meadows, also an ex-soldier from Fort Bragg, who was accused of driving Burmeister and Malcolm Wright, another white ex-soldier, to the area where the killings occurred, confessed and turned state's witness.

Meadows was arrested minutes after the shooting when a police officer saw him sitting in the car. He told police he heard six gunshots after Burmeister and Wright got out of the car. He also said Burmeister wanted to earn a "spider web" tattoo, a skinhead symbol police say represents the killing of a homosexual or a black person.
Police found white supremacist literature, a Nazi flag and a book on how to make a bomb in Burmeister's trailer home.

In the prosecutions case, Meadows testified Burmeister admitted killing the black couple and joked he was jailed for "performing a community service" while a former girlfriend of Burmeister's testified that he played music that glorified the killing of blacks and Jews.

Prosecutors ended the case showing pictures of a leather jacket with racist symbols they said was the defendant's. The jacket had a swastika sewn onto it and a reversed American flag with yellow border.
Wright, 22, of Lexington, Ky., will be tried in March for murder and conspiracy to commit murder charges. He also faces the death penalty.
